source.title: Just Enough Shifts: Mitigating Over-Refusal in Aligned Language Models with Targeted Representation Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Mahavir Dabas; Si Chen; Charles Fleming; Ming Jin; Ruoxi Jia

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a difference-in-means refusal direction and tests a different intervention: targeted, single-layer representation fine-tuning that shifts safe and harmful query activations relative to that direction, then evaluates refusal-related behavior and general capability. It does not apply the original all-layer, all-position ablation or addition.
record.gate_note: The refusal direction is computed from 64 harmful and 64 benign queries, and the selected layer is chosen by silhouette score; these are setup and selection values, not outcome rows. The reported uniform-shift breakdown is included because the paper explicitly describes its outcome. The main ACTOR benchmark and capability results are recorded separately by model and metric.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-in-means refusal direction from Arditi et al. as a tool. It builds ACTOR, a single-layer fine-tuning method that targets over-refusal, and reports only that method's compliance, safety and capability scores. It never tests whether ablating the direction removes refusal or adding it induces refusal, and it tests none of the other versions. The Surgical rows are another paper's method, run as a baseline. So the results speak to ACTOR's performance, not to whether any version of the claim holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that ACTOR, a projection-calibrated, single-layer activation-target fine-tuning method, reduces over-refusal while keeping AdvBench safety and general capability. They also argue it is more robust to the data used for the direction than fixed single-vector steering or ablation baselines.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal direction, but chooses a target layer using silhouette scores and applies query-specific, projection-scaled shifts through parameter fine-tuning at that layer; it does not perform the original all-layer, all-position projection ablation or inference-time addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected layer matters: the paper reports performance comparable to the default when using earlier or later layers instead of the chosen target layer. It also reports that uniform rather than projection-calibrated shifts degrade outputs. The paper reports model-dependent best α values: 0.0015, 0.003, and 0.0004 for Llama-2-7b-chat, Gemma-7b-it, and Llama-2-13b-chat, respectively.

fits_no_version.finding: At layer 13 of Llama-2-7b-chat, subtracting a minimal γ·R per over-refused benign query (line search over γ in 0.1 to 1) yields a compliant response. The needed γ correlates with projection magnitude (Pearson 0.63, Figure 3). This is a single-layer steering effect on pseudo-harmful queries, with no refusal rate reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-refusal on pseudo-harmful prompts can be flipped to compliance by a query-specific single-layer shift against the refusal direction, with magnitude tracking the projection.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-vector refusal methods are sensitive to the data used to compute the direction. Surgical's average compliance drops from 86.39% to 63.88% when its direction is computed from OKTest instead of OR-Bench. SCANS fluctuates across harmful sets (Figure 4 right).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The behavioural effect of a difference-in-means refusal vector depends strongly on the prompt distribution used to estimate it.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd ICML, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The paper reports no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for these outcomes. Compliance and safety judgments use GPT-4o. The authors note that benchmark labels reflect differing normative views and that the method requires white-box access. The direct V1 intervention described in the claim (all-layer, all-position ablation and vector addition) is not conducted.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant primary ACTOR or capability outcomes were omitted. Other baseline-method values in Table 2 are not separately included except the Surgical single-vector ablation results, which directly bear on single-vector removal.

untested.parts: No all-layer or all-position ablation measuring refusal on harmful prompts. No direction addition to induce refusal on harmless prompts. No test that one direction alone mediates refusal.
No weight-edit abliteration of released models.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training against ablation.
No test of an affine, cone or multi-direction structure.
No separation of a harmfulness representation from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct or variant transfer.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V1 'supports' labels are not justified. The study is a method paper that uses the refusal direction as an ingredient, and its outcomes are its own method's benchmark scores. No verdicts are given. The sensitivity to the direction's data source and the single-layer steering line search are recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly ablate the direction from every layer and position, add the direction at inference time, or test whether one direction alone mediates refusal independently of the targeted fine-tuning procedure.
No weight-edit conversion of an ablation or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the direction or of training against ablation for robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is better represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
Does not distinguish a harmfulness judgment representation from a refusal-decision representation.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other model-variant transfer test of the direction.
Does not compare how refusal-training procedures or training stages determine whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: The direction serves as a target for fine-tuning a single layer. The nearest thing to a test is the Fig. 3 line search, which subtracts gamma*R on over-refused queries but reports only a Pearson correlation of 0.63 and no refusal rate.

tranche.reason: The study borrows the Arditi et al. difference-in-means direction to build ACTOR. It reports only ACTOR's and the baselines' over-refusal compliance, safety and capability, and it never ablates or adds the direction to test whether it mediates refusal.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled rows have the right numbers but are linked to V1 with observed or partial states. For a T4 study with no verdicts, they should carry versions ['none'] and the state cannot_determine. Possible V1-adjacent items no row records: the Fig. 3 line search on Llama-2-7b-chat layer 13 (gamma*R subtraction flips over-refusals, r=0.63, no rate), and Surgical's Avg C.R falling from 86.39 to 63.88 when its direction is built from OKTest instead of OR-Bench.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ACTOR on the three evaluated aligned models, using its selected target layer
reader_labels.reason: The direction-guided fine-tuning raises benign-query compliance across the reported benchmarks, retains high AdvBench denial scores, and has mostly stable capability measures (r01–r48). The Surgical baseline also reports increased average compliance after single-vector ablation on the two models shown (r54–r57).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Uniform shifts and non-target-layer ACTOR settings
reader_labels.reason: Uniform-shift training reportedly produces nonsensical outputs, and changing ACTOR to layers 5 or 25 leaves average compliance near the default rather than producing the target-layer gains (r49, r51, r53).
